description: We are third- and fourth-year university students passionate about science and technology. We’re eager to learn and apply data analysis and machine learning methods to explore complex questions.
summary:
Which places on Earth could help us study the Moon and Mars? Regolith is an interactive atlas that brings together open Earth-observation and planetary data to find and compare potential terrestrial analogs.

We built a processing pipeline that harmonizes measurements from different instruments under a common feature contract, and trained an unsupervised machine learning model to explore similarities in terrain. The result is a tool that presents maps, references, similarity scores, and data-quality context to help guide further scientific review.

The atlas already supports exploration of a global sample and a regional case study in Nicaragua. Its modular design makes it possible to add new areas, data sources, and resolutions. With additional computing resources and suitable data, the approach could support denser sampling and finer-detail analysis around the world. Regolith turns dispersed scientific data into a reproducible search, while treating its results as research hypotheses—not confirmed analogs or certified mission sites.
details:
The problem

Earth's deserts, volcanic landscapes, and polar regions can help researchers investigate questions relevant to exploring the Moon and Mars. Finding useful sites, however, means bringing together measurements from different instruments, interpreting different scales and coverage, and examining a vast area. A visual resemblance alone is not enough to establish a scientific analog.

Our solution

Regolith transforms Earth and planetary observations into information that can be explored consistently. Users can select a reference—such as the Jezero fan on Mars or lunar polar sites—compare terrestrial windows, inspect candidates on maps, and review the sources and limitations behind the measurements. Our goal is to help researchers and exploration teams prioritize places for further study while preserving the traceability of each result.

For Nicaragua, we adapted the search around 13 volcanoes from the Smithsonian catalog and four sites studied in the scientific literature: Cerro Negro, Momotombo, Telica, and the San Jacinto geothermal field. The global grid was too sparse to represent these places well, so we added more closely spaced windows around volcanic areas. This allows a more detailed search where there is a specific scientific question. The published sites are scientific references because of their alteration processes; new matches suggested by the engine remain candidates that need independent investigation.

How it works

1. Acquire and organize open data. We use NASA HiRISE terrain data for Jezero, LOLA data for lunar references, Copernicus DEM GLO-30 for terrestrial surfaces, and ESA WorldCover and JRC Global Surface Water for land-cover context, among other sources.

2. Harmonize observations. Instrument-specific adapters convert products into a common feature contract that records units, spatial footprint, method, coverage, quality, and provenance. For topography, we calculate descriptors using compatible physical distances, including relative relief, slope, roughness, and shape. The shared contract makes it easier to integrate sources, but each addition still requires checks for resolution, support, and comparability.

3. Learn the structure of the data.We trained an unsupervised machine learning model on a reproducible sample of 200,000 terrestrial windows. We chose this approach because there were not enough independent labels of confirmed analogs for reliable supervised training. The model uses quantile transformations, robust covariance, and morphological regimes to compare related characteristics without relying on a single raw measurement.

4. Find and explain candidates. The engine calculates similarity across views and combines those with sufficient data, using explicit weights and a stated policy for missing information. The application lets users explore the results and their context. The global release also has a separate quantile-based topographic search; its ranking is distinct from the ML engine.

5. Review and refine. Land-cover layers allow the criteria to be adapted to the question. Candidates should be checked against imagery, additional measurements, and expert assessment. The system records missing information so that a lack of data is not confused with the absence of a property.

Scale and potential

In the documented release, we processed 1,793,175 windows in 22,308 batches; 1,459,470 met the topographic quality requirements for ranking. Each window covers 3 × 3 km and is processed on 30 m cells; the centers in the global grid are spaced 10 km apart. This is a sample with global reach, not continuous 30 m coverage of the entire planet.

Batch processing, tiled data, and partial reads allow us to create summaries without keeping all source files on disk at once. A benchmark using four workers showed that the tested workflow can operate at broad scale and that network throughput can be a limiting factor. The final model was trained on a Google Cloud virtual machine. These results support the feasibility of the workflow we tested; they do not establish that every global analysis can run on any machine or at a universal cost.

The feature contract and extraction modules provide a foundation for extending the system to new regions, sites of interest, and products without rebuilding the entire application. With more resources, we could make the sampling grid denser, process finer-resolution data, and extend global coverage. That would require suitable source data, additional computing, storage and transfer capacity, and renewed validation across sensors and scales: resampling an image does not create detail that the instrument never observed.

Current status and next steps

The experimental ranking currently uses primarily topographic characteristics. We have investigated spectral bridges between CRISM and EMIT and explored thermal and radar data, but those views are not fitted in the published model and should not be interpreted as part of its current score. Similar terrain does not establish equivalent mineralogy, geology, or habitability, and the tool does not assess a site's safety or accessibility. Independent blind validation is still pending.

Our next steps are to evaluate candidates with specialists and independent controls; measure ranking stability across sources and scales; complete and validate mineralogical, thermal, and radar dimensions; expand profiles for volcanic, coastal, and polar environments; and densify regions where a more detailed search adds value. We want Regolith to be a reproducible tool that connects open data, local knowledge, and future planetary research.

Tools used

We developed the processing pipeline and engine in Python, using scientific and geospatial libraries including GDAL, Rasterio, PROJ, NumPy, SciPy, and scikit-learn. DuckDB and Parquet support feature queries and storage. The application uses TypeScript, React, Vite, and CesiumJS, with FastAPI for data services. We worked on local machines and a Google Cloud virtual machine; the repository also includes cloud-operation configuration. The code, contracts, and data manifests make the methodology inspectable and support reproduction when the required inputs are available.
